questions.q: An emf is induced in a motor's coil as it rotates in the external magnetic field. In what direction does this induced emf act, and what is it called?
options: In the same direction as the supply emf, and it is called the driving emf
In the opposite direction to the input voltage or supply emf, and it is called the back emf
At right angles to the supply emf, and it is called the transverse emf
It acts only at the instant of switch-on and is called the starting emf
questions.explanation: The emf induced by the rotation of the motor's coil is in the opposite direction to the input voltage (the supply emf), so it is called the back emf. It opposes the supply because, if it did not, the current would increase and the coil would speed up without limit.

questions.q: How is the net voltage across the armature coil of a running motor related to the input voltage and the back emf?
options: Net voltage = input voltage + back emf
Net voltage = input voltage (or supply emf) minus the back emf
Net voltage = back emf minus the input voltage
Net voltage = input voltage multiplied by the back emf
questions.explanation: The net voltage across the coil equals the input voltage (or supply emf) minus the back emf. Because the armature coil has a fixed resistance, this net voltage determines the magnitude of the current that flows.

questions.q: The armature winding of an electric motor has a resistance of 10 ohms and is connected to a 240 V supply. What is the current that passes through the motor when it is first started?
questions.given: \(R = 10\,\Omega\),  supply \(V = 240\,\mathrm{V}\),  back emf \(= 0\) (coil not yet moving)
working: When the motor is first started there is no back emf, so the voltage drop across the motor is the full supply, \(240\,\mathrm{V}\).
questions.explanation: At start-up the coil is stationary, so the back emf is zero and the full 240 V drives current through the 10 ohm winding, giving a large 24 A surge.

questions.q: The same electric motor (armature resistance 10 ohms, 240 V supply) is operating with a normal load, when the back emf is equal to 232 V. What current passes through the motor when it is operating normally?
working: Voltage drop across the motor = input voltage minus the back emf
questions.explanation: Running normally, the 232 V back emf opposes the supply, leaving only 8 V net to drive current through the 10 ohm winding, so I = 0.8 A. This shows motors require large currents when starting compared with when operating normally.

questions.q: The induced emf in a motor's coil is in the opposite direction to the supply emf. What would happen if this were not the case?
options: The motor would stop immediately
The current would increase and the motor coil would go faster and faster forever
The resistance of the coil would rise until no current flowed
The supply emf would be cancelled and the motor would draw no current
questions.explanation: If the induced emf did not oppose the supply, the current would increase and the motor coil would go faster and faster forever. That would create energy from nothing, so conservation of energy requires the back emf to oppose the supply.

questions.q: If nothing is attached to slow an electric motor (ignoring friction), what happens to the armature coil and its current as it speeds up?
options: The speed rises until the back emf equals the external emf, so there is no voltage across the coil and no current flows
The speed rises until the current reaches a maximum and stays there
The back emf falls to zero and the current rises without limit
The coil reaches a fixed speed set only by the friction in the bearings
questions.explanation: With no load, the speed of the armature coil increases until the back emf is equal to the external emf. When this occurs there is no voltage across the coil and therefore no current, no net force, and the armature rotates at a constant rate.

questions.q: The armature coil of a motor has a fixed resistance. State how the back emf controls the current, and explain what this means for an overloaded motor.
keyPoints: Since the armature coil has a fixed resistance, the net voltage across it determines the magnitude of the current that flows.
The smaller the back emf is, the greater the current flowing through the coil.
An overloaded motor rotates too slowly, so the back emf is reduced and the voltage across the coil remains high, giving a high current that could burn out the motor.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that a smaller back emf means a larger current, and tied overloading (slow rotation, low back emf, high current) to burning out the motor, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: How are motors usually protected from the initially high currents produced when they are switched on?
options: By a capacitor placed in parallel with the armature coil
By a series resistor that is switched out of the circuit at higher speeds, because the back emf then results in a lower current
By reversing the supply polarity at the instant of switch-on
By using slip rings instead of a split-ring commutator
questions.explanation: Motors are usually protected from the high switch-on currents by a series resistor. Once the motor is up to speed, the back emf itself limits the current, so the resistor is switched out of the circuit because it would only waste energy.

questions.q: From memory, recite the causal chain that produces back-EMF in a DC motor, naming each law in order.
keyPoints: The supply current in the field makes the coil spin (motor effect), and the spinning coil experiences a continuously changing magnetic flux.
By Faraday's law, the changing flux induces an emf in the coil; the faster the coil spins, the larger the induced emf.
By Lenz's law, that induced emf opposes the change driving it, so it opposes the supply voltage - this is the back-EMF.
It must oppose because of conservation of energy (otherwise the motor would accelerate without limit). Mnemonic: 'Faraday makes it, Lenz flips it.'
questions.explanation: The five links are: motor effect, changing flux, Faraday, Lenz, energy conservation. If you named Faraday and Lenz in the right order and linked the opposition to conservation of energy, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: Explain how back-EMF makes a DC motor self-regulating when the mechanical load on it suddenly increases. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: When the load increases, the motor slows down. A slower coil changes its flux less rapidly, so by Faraday's law the back-EMF falls. Because the current equals the supply voltage minus the back-EMF divided by the armature resistance, a smaller back-EMF means a larger net voltage and therefore a larger current. By the motor effect (F = BIL), this larger current produces a larger force and hence greater torque - exactly the extra torque needed to drive the heavier load. The motor responds automatically without any external adjustment, which is why it is described as self-regulating.

criteria.descriptor: States that a heavier load slows the motor, reducing the back-EMF (via slower changing flux / Faraday's law).
Links the smaller back-EMF to a larger net voltage and hence larger current (I = (V - back-EMF)/R).
Concludes the larger current gives greater torque (F = BIL), matching the load, so the motor is self-regulating.

questions.explanation: The marker rewards the feedback loop: more load to slower speed to lower back-EMF to higher current to more torque, all happening automatically.
